seo_description: Is a one-page or two-page resume better? Use simple rules by experience level and field, and learn how to trim or extend your resume without padding.
tags: how long should a resume be
content:
A one-page resume is the right choice for students, freshers and anyone with a few years of focused experience. A two-page resume suits professionals with a longer, relevant history. The best length is the shortest one that clearly shows why you fit the job, with no padding and no tiny fonts.

## Why length is a real decision

Recruiters spend limited time on each resume, so every extra line competes with the ones above it. A bloated resume buries your best evidence. A resume that is too thin can leave out key proof. Length is therefore a question of selection: what does this particular reader need to see?

Rules of thumb exist because they are useful, but they are not laws. The test is whether each line helps you win an interview for this role.

## A practical guide by situation

### Students and freshers

Use **one page**. You likely have education, a few projects, skills and some activities, which fit comfortably. A second page would mean padding.

### Early-career professionals (roughly up to five years)

Use **one page** in most cases. Focus on the last two or three roles and strongest results. If you are a strong fit with unusually relevant projects, a few extra lines are acceptable, but trim before you add a page.

### Mid-career and senior professionals

Use **one to two pages**. If you have many years of relevant experience, multiple roles and significant achievements, two pages are normal. Make sure page one carries the strongest evidence, because some readers will not reach page two.

### Academic, research and some technical roles

Fields with publications, grants, patents or long project lists may use longer CV formats. Follow the conventions of your field and the employer's instructions. If they ask for a CV, check what they expect.

### Career changers

Keep to **one page** if possible. You are showing transferable highlights, not your entire history. See our guide on career change resumes for how to select.

## How to trim to one page

If your resume spills onto a second page, edit before you format:

1. **Delete the weakest bullets.** Remove duties that anyone in the role would have.
2. **Merge related points.** Two small bullets can often become one clear one.
3. **Shorten old roles.** Jobs from many years ago can have one or two lines.
4. **Cut irrelevant sections.** Hobbies, references and "available on request" lines can go.
5. **Tighten wording.** Replace phrases with single words ("in charge of" becomes "led").
6. **Adjust layout last.** Slightly smaller margins or spacing can help, but keep fonts readable.

Never rely on tiny text. If your resume is difficult to read on screen, it is too crowded.

## How to extend to two pages responsibly

If you have strong, relevant content that would not fit, a second page is fine, provided you follow these guidelines:

- Fill at least about half of page two; a few stray lines look unfinished.
- Put your best material on page one, including the summary and most recent role.
- Add your name and page number in the document so loose pages can be identified. (Keep contact details in the main body rather than only the header.)
- Group older or less relevant roles on page two.
- Include extras such as certifications, publications or projects only if they support the target role.

## Quality beats quantity

Adding more pages does not make you more qualified. Evidence does. Before adding a new bullet, ask: does this prove a skill the job needs? Does it show a different skill from the bullets I already have? If not, leave it out.

### A prompt to help you cut

```
Here is my resume and the job description I am applying for. I need to
reduce the resume to [one page / about 600 words]. Rank each bullet and
section from most to least relevant to the job, and suggest which to cut,
merge or shorten. Do not rewrite facts or add new content. Explain your
reasoning briefly.

Resume: [paste]
Job description: [paste]
```

This gives you a prioritised list, but the final selection should reflect your judgement.

## Layout choices that help you fit

- Use a clean single-column layout with consistent spacing.
- Choose a font size you can read comfortably when printed.
- Put dates and locations on the same line as titles to save space.
- Use short section headings.
- Avoid large headers, big photos or graphics that waste space.

You can preview how much fits in different layouts using the [resume templates](/resume-templates), and then edit content in the [resume builder](/resume-builder).

### Thinking about page breaks

If you do have two pages, avoid breaking a job entry in a way that leaves the title at the bottom of page one and the bullets on page two. In a PDF export, check where the page falls. It is a small detail that makes the document feel professional. Our article comparing PDF and DOCX files explains why exporting and checking the final layout matters.

### A quick self-test before you decide

Answer these questions honestly:

1. Does every bullet on my resume support the specific job I am applying for?
2. Could a reader skip any section without losing something important?
3. If I removed my oldest role, would the resume still tell the same story?
4. Is anything on page two stronger evidence than something on page one?
5. Would I be comfortable discussing every line for five minutes in an interview?

If you answered "no" to the first question or "yes" to the second, edit further. If your content genuinely passes all five checks and still runs to two pages, you have a justified two-page resume.

### Tailoring length per application

Length can change with the role. A resume for a specialist position that values depth may reasonably use two pages, while a resume for a general entry-level role should be tighter. Keep a longer master version and create shorter, targeted ones. This approach saves effort and ensures each submission stays focused on what the employer wants to see.

## Common mistakes

- **Cramming with tiny fonts and thin margins.** It repels readers.
- **Including every job ever held.** Select what supports the target role.
- **Padding with filler.** Vague statements add length without value.
- **Putting key achievements on page two only.** Many readers will not get there.
- **Treating one page as an absolute rule.** A well-justified second page is acceptable.
- **Forgetting to re-check after edits.** Small changes can push content onto a new page.

## Next steps

Choose a layout in the [resume templates](/resume-templates), edit your content in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and confirm the final PDF reads cleanly using the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker).

faq.q: Is a one-page resume always better?
faq.a: No. One page is ideal for students, freshers and people with limited or highly focused experience. Professionals with many years of relevant work may need two pages. Length should depend on how much relevant evidence you have, not on a rigid rule.

faq.q: Is a two-page resume bad?
faq.a: Not at all, if every line earns its place. A well-organised two-page resume is common for experienced professionals. Problems arise when the second page holds only a few lines, or when the whole document is padded with old or irrelevant detail.

faq.q: How far back should my work history go?
faq.a: Many people go back about ten to fifteen years, focusing on relevant roles. Older jobs can be shortened or summarised in a line. Keep early roles if they are directly relevant to the position you want.

faq.q: Do I need to shrink the font to fit one page?
faq.a: Avoid shrinking text and margins to squeeze content in. Cut lower-value material instead. A readable font size and sensible margins matter more than cramming every item onto a single page.

title: Cover Letter Structure: A Simple Four-Paragraph Format
excerpt: Follow a clear cover letter structure: a focused opening, evidence paragraphs, a company connection and a confident close. Includes a template and a prompt.
seo_title: Cover Letter Structure: A Simple Four-Paragraph Format
seo_description: Learn how to structure a cover letter in four short paragraphs. Get a copy-ready template, tips for each part and a prompt for drafting without clichés.
tags: how to write a cover letter
content:
A strong cover letter has four short parts: an opening that names the role and your fit, one or two paragraphs of evidence, a paragraph connecting you to the employer, and a confident close. Aim for around 250 to 350 words, address the reader by name where possible, and say something your resume does not.

## What a cover letter is for

Your resume lists facts. A cover letter explains why those facts matter for this particular job. It is your chance to show that you understand the role, to connect two or three of your best examples to what the employer needs and to give a sense of how you communicate.

It is not a second copy of your resume, a life story or a form letter. Hiring managers can spot a generic letter within a line or two, and it rarely helps. The most useful letters are specific, brief and honest.

## The overall layout

Keep the format clean:

- Your name and contact details at the top (matching your resume)
- Date, if sending as a document
- The employer's name and company, if known
- Greeting
- Four short paragraphs
- Sign-off and your name

Use a plain font, normal margins and a single page. If you are pasting into an email or application form, skip the address blocks and begin with the greeting.

## The four paragraphs, one by one

### Paragraph 1: The opening

Open with the role, a clear statement of interest and your strongest reason for fitting. Aim for two or three sentences. Skip generic lines like "I am writing to apply for the position of..." if you can replace them with something sharper.

**Weak:** "I am writing to apply for the Marketing Assistant position at your company."

**Stronger:** "I would like to apply for the Marketing Assistant role. In my last two years running a student society's social channels, I planned weekly content and reported results to a committee, which is closely aligned with the work described in your posting."

The stronger version names the role, gives a real credential and connects to the job.

### Paragraph 2 (and optionally 3): The evidence

This is the heart of the letter. Choose two or three requirements from the job description and tell a short story for each: what the situation was, what you did and what happened. Use the same honest approach as in your resume bullets: no invented numbers, no inflated titles.

A simple pattern:

> When [situation or task], I [action you took], which [result or lesson]. That experience would help me [how it applies to this role].

Example:

> When our society's event signups dropped, I rewrote the invitation emails and added a short reminder a week before each event. Attendance improved at the following events, and I learned to test small changes and check results. That approach would help me support your campaign planning.

If the result is not measurable, describe the effect in words, and do not make up a figure.

### Paragraph 3: The employer connection

Show you know who you are writing to. Mention something specific and accurate about the organisation: a product, a project, a value stated on its site, a type of customer. Then link it to your motivation.

Avoid flattery that could apply anywhere ("I admire your innovative culture"). Instead, say what you noticed and why it matters to you: "I was interested to see that your team publishes beginner guides for new customers; I enjoy explaining technical topics simply, and I would like to contribute to that work."

If you cannot find specific information, spend ten minutes reading the company's website and recent public updates. Do not claim insider knowledge you lack.

### Paragraph 4: The close

End with a confident, polite summary and a clear next step:

> Thank you for considering my application. I have attached my resume and would welcome the chance to discuss how I can contribute to your team. I am available for a conversation at your convenience.

Sign off with a professional closing such as "Sincerely" or "Kind regards", followed by your name.

## A copy-ready template

```
Dear [Name / Hiring Team],

I would like to apply for the [job title] role at [company]. [One sentence
naming your strongest relevant credential or experience.]

[Short story 1: situation, action, result, link to the role.]

[Short story 2 or a relevant skill or project, linked to a requirement
in the posting.]

[Why this company or team, mentioning something specific and accurate.
Connect it to your motivation.]

Thank you for considering my application. I have attached my resume and
would welcome the opportunity to discuss the role further.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Phone] | [Email]
```

### A prompt to draft a first version

```
Draft a one-page cover letter of about 280 words for a [job title] role at
[company]. Use this structure: opening, two evidence paragraphs, a paragraph
about why this company, and a polite close. Use ONLY the facts below.
Avoid clichés such as "passionate", "dynamic" and "I believe I would be a
great fit". Do not invent numbers or achievements. Mark any place where
I need to add a real detail with [BRACKETS].

Job description: [paste]
My relevant experience: [paste]
What I know about the company: [paste]
```

Edit the draft heavily so that it sounds like you. You can also start from a structured form with the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

## Style tips

- **Write like you speak in a professional meeting:** clear, direct and warm.
- **Vary sentence openings** so every sentence does not start with "I".
- **Use active verbs** and concrete nouns.
- **Keep paragraphs short**, three to five lines.
- **Read it aloud** to catch stiffness and mistakes.
- **Match the tone** to the field. A creative role can allow more personality than a legal or finance role.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending a generic letter.** If the company name could be swapped without changing a word, rewrite it.
- **Repeating the resume.** Add context and stories instead.
- **Opening with an apology.** "Although I lack experience" starts you on the back foot. Lead with strengths.
- **Being too long.** More than one page rarely helps.
- **Making unsupported claims.** Statements like "I am the perfect candidate" need evidence, or they sound empty.
- **Forgetting the details.** Wrong company names, wrong job titles and leftover template text are serious errors.
- **Skipping proofreading.** Read it twice and ask someone else to check it if you can.

## Next steps

Draft your letter in the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder), make sure your [resume](/resume-builder) tells the same story, and compare your wording to the posting with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) to see which requirements to feature.

faq.q: How long should a cover letter be?
faq.a: Aim for about 250 to 350 words, which fits comfortably on one page with space for a greeting and sign-off. Shorter is fine if you are applying through an email body. Every sentence should add something your resume does not already say.

faq.q: Do I need to address the hiring manager by name?
faq.a: If the name is easy to find on the job posting or company page, use it. If not, a neutral greeting such as "Dear Hiring Team" is acceptable. Avoid outdated phrases like "To Whom It May Concern" when you can.

faq.q: Should my cover letter repeat my resume?
faq.a: No. Use it to add context and selected proof: why you want this role, two or three relevant achievements told briefly, and how you would contribute. Reference your resume rather than restating it line by line.

faq.q: Are cover letters still necessary?
faq.a: It depends on the employer. Some require them, others treat them as optional. When a posting asks for one, send it. When optional, a short, tailored letter can help, especially if you are changing fields or have a story your resume cannot tell.

title: 15 Common Resume Mistakes and Simple Ways to Fix Each One
excerpt: Spot and fix the resume mistakes that quietly cost interviews, from vague bullets and typos to messy formatting, with before-and-after fixes and a checklist.
seo_title: 15 Common Resume Mistakes and How to Fix Them
seo_description: Avoid the resume mistakes that cost interviews. Learn 15 common errors, from vague bullets to messy formatting, and how to fix each one with simple examples.
content:
The most common resume mistakes are vague bullets, typos, inconsistent formatting, missing keywords from the job posting and including irrelevant detail. Each is easy to fix once you spot it. Use the 15 problems below as an audit of your own resume, and fix the ones that apply before your next application.

## The 15 mistakes, grouped

### Content mistakes

#### 1. Listing duties instead of contributions

"Responsible for customer service" tells the reader what the job was. Replace it with what you did: "Resolved billing questions by phone and chat, escalating complex cases with clear notes."

#### 2. Vague bullets with no scope or result

"Helped with projects" could mean anything. Add the project type, your role and the outcome: "Prepared slides and research summaries for three client proposals."

#### 3. Invented or inflated claims

Padding your role or inventing numbers is risky. Interviewers ask follow-up questions, and background checks verify facts. Describe your real contribution clearly; it is enough.

#### 4. Including everything you have ever done

A resume is a selection, not an archive. If a job from many years ago or a minor task does not support your target role, shorten or remove it.

#### 5. Ignoring the job posting

A resume that could be sent to any employer rarely stands out. Adjust your summary, skills order and top bullets to echo the posting's requirements where truthful. Our guide on finding keywords in a job description shows how.

### Language mistakes

#### 6. Clichés and empty adjectives

Terms like "hard-working", "team player" and "results-driven" claim without proving. Replace them with an example: "Coordinated a team of four to deliver a project two days before the deadline" (if true).

#### 7. Inconsistent tense and style

Use past tense for finished roles and present tense for your current role. Keep bullet structure parallel, so each line starts with an action verb.

#### 8. Typos and grammar errors

Spell-checkers miss correctly spelled wrong words ("manger" for "manager"). Read your resume slowly, read it aloud, change the font temporarily to see it differently and ask a friend to check it.

#### 9. Overlong sentences and dense paragraphs

Bullets should be one or two lines. If a point runs to three or four lines, split it or cut the extra detail.

### Formatting mistakes

#### 10. Cluttered or inconsistent layout

Different fonts, uneven spacing and mismatched date formats make a resume feel careless. Pick one font family, one date style and consistent spacing.

#### 11. Hard-to-parse design

Text in images, columns, tables or graphics can scramble in application systems. Use a clean, single-column layout with standard headings. The [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can flag structural issues.

#### 12. Wrong length

A fresher with a two-page resume or a senior professional with a cramped, tiny-font single page both struggle. See our one-page versus two-page guide for how to decide.

#### 13. Unprofessional details

Use a simple, name-based email address, a working phone number and a clear subject line when emailing. Remove irrelevant personal details unless your region or the employer's instructions require them.

### Process mistakes

#### 14. Sending the wrong file or a badly named one

Check that the file opens, the text is selectable and the name is sensible, such as `firstname-lastname-resume.pdf`. Follow the employer's instructions on file type. Our PDF versus DOCX comparison covers how to choose.

#### 15. Not proofreading the final exported file

Formatting can shift when you export. Open the exported PDF, scroll through every page, and check fonts, spacing, links and page breaks before sending.

## A quick before-and-after

**Before:**

> Responsible for managing social media accounts and helping with marketing tasks. Hard-working team player with good communication skills.

**After:**

> Planned and scheduled three weekly posts for two social accounts using a content calendar, and compiled monthly engagement summaries for the marketing lead.

The second version drops the clichés, adds scope and shows what you actually did.

### A prompt to audit your resume

```
Act as a strict but fair resume reviewer. Below is my resume and the job
description I am targeting. List the 10 most important problems, ranked by
impact, covering: vague bullets, missing relevant keywords, inconsistent
formatting, tense errors, typos and anything unclear. For each, quote the
text and suggest a fix that uses only facts already in my resume. Do not
add new experience, skills or numbers.

Resume: [paste]
Job description: [paste]
```

Read each suggestion critically. If a fix requires information you did not provide, treat it as a question for you to answer, not an instruction.

## A final checklist

- Every bullet starts with a verb and shows what you did.
- Top third of page one matches the job's main requirements.
- Dates, fonts and spacing are consistent.
- No typos in names, companies or contact details.
- Links work and the email address is professional.
- File name and type are sensible and accepted by the employer.
- You can talk about every line in an interview.

## How to find your own mistakes faster

You are the worst person to proofread your own resume, because your brain fills in what you meant to write. Try these methods to see it freshly:

- **Wait a day.** Even a few hours away from the document helps you notice errors.
- **Read it backwards,** line by line, to check spelling without getting caught up in the meaning.
- **Print it.** Mistakes that hide on screen often jump out on paper.
- **Change the font and size temporarily.** The unfamiliar look makes you read slowly.
- **Use text-to-speech.** Hearing the document read aloud highlights clumsy wording and missing words.
- **Ask a friendly reader** who is not in your field. If they cannot say what you do after one minute, simplify.

## Prioritise by impact

Not every mistake costs the same. If you have limited time, fix them in this order: contact details and typos first, then vague bullets in your most recent roles, then missing keywords for the target job, then layout and consistency. A resume with sharp bullets and a few small spacing quirks will do better than a perfectly spaced resume full of duties.

## Common mistakes

- **Over-editing and losing your voice.** Aim for clarity, not a robotic style.
- **Making the same fix everywhere.** Swapping every verb for a fancy synonym looks unnatural.
- **Fixing the design but not the content.** A beautiful template cannot rescue vague bullets.
- **Skipping a final read after edits.** New errors creep in when you change things.

## Next steps

Rebuild a clean version in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), compare layouts in the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and run a final structural check with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) before you hit send.

faq.q: What is the most common resume mistake?
faq.a: Describing duties instead of contributions is among the most common. Lines like "responsible for customer service" tell a reader what the job was, not what you did. Rewrite with specific actions and results that you can truthfully support.

faq.q: Do typos really matter on a resume?
faq.a: Yes. A typo suggests carelessness, which matters in almost any role, and when many applicants are similar it can be a deciding detail. Proofread slowly, read it aloud and ask someone else to check it before you submit.

faq.q: Should I include references on my resume?
faq.a: Usually not. Employers ask for references later, so "references available on request" wastes space. Prepare a separate list of people who have agreed to speak for you and share it when asked.

faq.q: Is it a mistake to use a creative template?
faq.a: It can be if the design hides text, uses columns or relies on images that software cannot read. You can use a tasteful layout, but make sure the text is selectable and the reading order is clear. Check how it looks when pasted into plain text.

title: Student Internship Resume: What to Include and How to Write It
excerpt: Build a student internship resume that highlights coursework, projects, clubs and skills. Includes section order, example bullets and a prompt to get started.
seo_title: Student Internship Resume: What to Include and Write
seo_description: Write a student internship resume that stands out without work history. Learn what to include, how to word projects and coursework, and how to tailor it.
content:
A student internship resume should fit on one page and lead with education, relevant coursework, projects and skills, followed by any work, volunteering or club roles. Describe what you did and produced, not just where you were. Tailor the order and wording to the internship description, and be accurate about everything you list.

## What internship recruiters are looking for

People hiring interns know you have limited experience. They are checking for signs that you are curious, reliable and capable of learning the work. They want to see that you have used relevant tools, finished projects, worked with others and communicated clearly. Your resume provides that evidence through coursework, projects, activities and any jobs you have held.

Because many applicants have similar academic backgrounds, specifics are what set resumes apart: what you built, how you worked with a team, what tools you used and what you learned.

## The recommended section order

1. **Header:** name, email, phone, city, a portfolio or professional profile link.
2. **Summary (optional):** two lines on your field, target internship and strengths.
3. **Education:** university, degree, expected graduation, relevant coursework and honours.
4. **Projects:** two to four, with brief bullets.
5. **Experience:** internships, part-time jobs, volunteering and club roles.
6. **Skills:** tools, methods and languages, grouped.
7. **Additional:** certifications, competitions or leadership, if relevant.

If you have a relevant previous internship, you might move Experience above Projects.

## What to put in each section

### Education: make it useful

List your degree, university and expected graduation date. Add:

- **Relevant coursework:** four to six courses that match the internship.
- **Academic projects or a thesis:** a one-line description if impressive.
- **Honours or scholarships:** only those you truly received.
- **GPA or marks:** if requested or strong.

Do not include every module you have taken. Select what is relevant, such as statistics for a data internship or marketing principles for a marketing placement.

### Projects: your best proof

Treat projects as mini job entries. Give each a title, the context (course, club, personal) and two or three bullets focused on your actions and results.

```
Customer Survey Analysis | Marketing course project | Apr 2025
- Designed a 10-question survey, gathered responses from classmates and cleaned the data in a spreadsheet
- Created three charts summarising findings and presented recommendations to a class of 25
- Wrote a two-page report explaining the methods and limitations
```

Be careful with group projects. State clearly what you did personally: "Built the data-cleaning script" is more useful than "worked on a team project".

### Experience, clubs and volunteering

Count any role where you took responsibility:

- **Part-time jobs:** even non-related roles show reliability and customer or teamwork skills. Keep descriptions brief and highlight transferable points.
- **Club or society roles:** treasurer, social media manager, event coordinator.
- **Volunteering:** tutoring, community drives, fundraising events.
- **Freelance or small tasks:** designing posters, building a simple website, translating documents.

Example bullet: "Managed a club budget with a spreadsheet, tracked member payments and prepared a summary for the committee at the end of each term."

### Skills section for students

Group skills in plain text. A student might list:

```
Software: Excel, Google Workspace, Canva, Git
Languages: Python (intermediate), SQL (basic), English (fluent)
Methods: survey design, data cleaning, presentation, teamwork
```

Label levels honestly. If a posting requires a skill you are still learning, you can write "learning" next to it, or leave it out and mention your plan in your cover letter. For more detail, see our guide to the skills section.

## Tailor it to each internship

Read the internship description and choose which projects, coursework and skills to emphasise. If a data internship stresses spreadsheets and reporting, move your analytical project to the top. If a marketing internship mentions social media, bring forward your club's channel management.

Adjust a few keywords where they truthfully match your experience. The guide on finding keywords in a job description explains the process.

### A prompt to start your student resume

```
I am a [year] student in [major] applying for a [field] internship.
Below are my courses, projects, activities and skills. Turn each project and
activity into 2-3 resume bullets starting with an action verb. Use only
the facts I provide, do not add numbers or tools I did not mention, and ask
me questions where details are missing. Then suggest the best order of
sections for this internship.

[PASTE DETAILS]
[PASTE INTERNSHIP DESCRIPTION]
```

Keep control of the facts, and edit the language into your own voice.

## Formatting for students

- Stay to **one page**.
- Use a simple single-column layout with standard headings so it parses well.
- Use a professional email address.
- Save as a PDF unless told otherwise.
- Check hyperlinks if you include a portfolio or repository.

The [resume templates](/resume-templates) include clean student-friendly layouts, and the [resume builder](/resume-builder) lets you move sections as you tailor.

### Pair it with a short cover letter

An internship application often benefits from a brief letter that explains why you want the role and highlights one or two projects. The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can help you structure it.

### A sample structure you can copy

Here is a skeleton for a one-page student resume. Fill each bracket with your own real information and delete anything that does not apply.

```
[FULL NAME]
City, Country | email | phone | portfolio link

SUMMARY
[Year] [major] student with project experience in [area]. Seeking a
[field] internship to apply [skills] and learn from [type of team].

EDUCATION
[Degree], [University] | Expected [month year]
Relevant coursework: [4-6 courses]

PROJECTS
[Project 1] | [Context] | [Date]
- [Action verb + what you did + tool + output]
- [Action verb + what you did + tool + output]

EXPERIENCE AND ACTIVITIES
[Role], [Organisation] | [Dates]
- [Responsibility or result]

SKILLS
Software: [list] | Methods: [list] | Languages: [list]
```

### Timing and preparation

Many internship programmes open applications months before the start date, so begin your resume early. Ask a lecturer or career adviser for feedback, visit your university's career services if they offer resume reviews and keep a running list of projects and responsibilities as they happen. That list will save you hours when deadlines arrive.

Also prepare for the interview that follows: for each project on your resume, be ready to explain the goal, your role, a challenge you met and what you learned. If you cannot talk about it for two minutes, trim it or practise first.

## Common mistakes

- **Listing duties without detail.** "Member of the marketing club" says little. Say what you did.
- **Using a long objective statement.** Replace it with a short, specific summary or skip it.
- **Overstating group projects.** Be clear about your personal contribution.
- **Including irrelevant hobbies.** Use the space for things that support the internship.
- **Skipping tailoring.** Send a version adapted to each posting.
- **Neglecting file names.** Use something like `firstname-lastname-resume.pdf`.
- **Leaving out links.** If you have a project repository or portfolio, link to it.

## Next steps

Create your one-page draft in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), choose a layout from the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and test the finished file with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) before applying.

faq.q: What should a student put on an internship resume?
faq.a: Include education, relevant coursework, projects, skills, clubs or volunteering, and any part-time work. Describe what you did and produced in each, using action verbs and honest detail. Tailor the order to emphasise what matches the internship description.

faq.q: Should I include my GPA on an internship resume?
faq.a: Include it if the employer asks for it, or if it is strong by the standard in your country and field. If it is not a strength, leave it out and focus on projects, skills and activities. Never change or round up figures.

faq.q: Can I include high school activities?
faq.a: For first- and second-year students, a few strong high school items can be fine if they show leadership, achievement or a relevant skill. As you gain university projects and experience, replace older items with more recent and relevant ones.

faq.q: How long should an internship resume be?
faq.a: One page. Internship recruiters expect concise resumes from students, and a single focused page forces you to keep only the most relevant evidence. If you are running over, cut weaker or older items first.

title: How to Use AI to Tailor Your Resume Honestly and Safely
excerpt: Use AI to tailor your resume to a job description without inventing experience. Learn a safe workflow, example prompts and the checks that keep it truthful.
seo_title: Use AI to Tailor Your Resume Honestly and Safely
seo_description: Tailor your resume with AI without fabricating anything. Follow a step-by-step workflow, copy safe prompts and use a checklist to keep every claim truthful.
content:
You can use AI to tailor your resume honestly by giving it your real experience and the job description, asking it only to reorder, reword and highlight relevant points, and then checking every line against the truth. The assistant is an editor, not a source of facts. If it adds anything you did not provide, delete it.

## What AI is good at, and what it is not

AI tools are useful for tasks like comparing a resume with a job description, suggesting which bullets to move up, rewording a clumsy line and spotting inconsistent tense. They can save time and help you see your own experience from a recruiter's viewpoint.

They are not reliable sources of fact about you. Assistants may produce confident, plausible text that includes tools you did not use, results that never happened or titles you never held. Everything on your resume must come from you. The ethical and practical rule is simple: if you cannot explain it in an interview, it does not belong on the page.

## Protect your privacy first

Before pasting anything into a tool:

- Remove your phone number, home address, date of birth and any ID numbers.
- Consider replacing the employer's confidential details with general descriptions.
- Check the provider's privacy and data settings to understand how inputs are handled.

You can add contact details back in your own document when you finalise it.

## A safe workflow in six steps

### Step 1: Prepare a master resume

Keep one complete document with all your roles, achievements, projects, tools and certifications. This is your source of truth. Tailored versions are always drawn from it.

### Step 2: Analyse the job description

Ask the assistant to extract requirements, not to write anything yet.

```
Read the job description below. List: (1) the top 8 responsibilities,
(2) required skills and tools, (3) preferred skills, and (4) words
the employer repeats. Do not add anything not in the text.

[PASTE JOB DESCRIPTION]
```

### Step 3: Map your experience to the requirements

```
Here is my master resume and the requirements from above. Create a table:
for each requirement, quote the lines in my resume that provide evidence,
or write "no evidence found". Do not invent or infer experience I have
not stated.

[PASTE MASTER RESUME TEXT]
```

The "no evidence found" rows are important. They show gaps to address honestly, rather than hide.

### Step 4: Reorder and reword

```
Using only the facts in my master resume, produce a tailored version for
this job. You may reorder bullets, change wording to use the employer's
terminology where it accurately describes my work, and shorten text.
You may NOT add skills, tools, employers, dates, numbers or achievements.
If a bullet could be improved with extra detail, add a question for me
instead of making up the detail.
```

### Step 5: Verify every line

Compare the tailored version with your master. Highlight anything new. For each new phrase ask: did I really do this? Can I explain it? Is the number accurate? Remove anything that fails.

### Step 6: Read it as yourself

Read aloud. Does it sound like you? Replace stiff phrases with your normal professional voice. Keep specific details and real examples; they make the resume memorable and credible.

## Use AI to find gaps, not fill them with fiction

If the job needs a skill you do not have, you have three honest options:

1. Point to related experience that supports it, if it exists.
2. State that you are learning it, if you really are.
3. Leave it out and apply anyway if the match is otherwise strong, or choose another role.

The [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can show you which terms from a posting are absent from your text, so you can decide what to do about each one.

## Tailor the cover letter too

The same rules apply to letters. Provide your facts and the job description, ask for a draft that uses only those facts, and then edit it. Many people find it useful to ask the assistant to list two or three of their experiences that best match the role, then choose which to tell as stories. The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can structure the final letter.

### What a good tailored result looks like

A well-tailored resume usually has these features:

- The summary names the target role or focus in plain terms.
- The top bullets in each job match the employer's main priorities.
- Skills are ordered by relevance and use the employer's terms where honest.
- Nothing appears that is absent from your master document.
- The language still sounds like a real person.

## Sample before-and-after, using only real facts

Suppose your master resume says: "Handled customer emails and updated the order spreadsheet." The job posting stresses "customer communication" and "data accuracy".

An honest tailored version might read: "Responded to customer emails and kept the order spreadsheet accurate and up to date, flagging mismatches to the team lead." Notice that the fact base is the same. The wording now echoes the posting, and the detail about flagging mismatches appears only if it genuinely happened. If you did not flag mismatches, the assistant should have asked you instead of adding it.

### Warning signs that the output has gone too far

Watch for these red flags when reviewing an AI draft:

- A tool, platform or certification you never mentioned
- A number, percentage or time-saving figure that is not in your notes
- A job title that is more senior than your real one
- Words like "spearheaded" or "pioneered" for tasks you simply took part in
- Responsibilities that sound like the job description rather than your own work

If any of these appear, remove them and re-run the prompt with a stricter instruction. Keeping a short list of "facts I can prove" next to the draft makes the check faster.

### Keep your own judgement in charge

The assistant can suggest, but it does not know your career story, your industry norms or what you are comfortable defending. Use it for speed and perspective, and rely on your own judgement for truth and tone.

## Common mistakes

- **Letting the assistant "improve" with invented detail.** Always restrict it to your facts.
- **Pasting the output without reading it.** Errors and clichés slip through.
- **Copying the job description's phrases wholesale.** Use the terms, not the sentences.
- **Over-polishing.** A resume full of buzzwords reads as generic.
- **Sharing sensitive information.** Remove private data before pasting.
- **Using the same AI output for every job.** Tailor each time, from your master.
- **Forgetting to update the master.** When you gain real new experience, add it.

### A last responsibility check

Treat AI the way you would treat a friend who helps with your resume: grateful for the ideas, but you sign your name at the end. If an employer later asks about any claim, you should be able to answer comfortably and truthfully.

## Next steps

Keep your master document in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), create tailored versions for each application, test them with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) and explore more prompts in the [careers prompt library](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: Is it okay to use AI to write my resume?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the content is true and you review it. AI can help you organise, reword and tailor, but you remain responsible for every claim. Never let it add skills, employers, dates or numbers that you cannot back up.

faq.q: Will employers know I used AI?
faq.a: They may notice generic, overly polished wording. The best protection is to supply your real details, edit the output into your own voice and keep specifics that only you would know. Honest, specific resumes read as human.

faq.q: Should I upload my full resume with personal details?
faq.a: Be cautious. Remove sensitive information such as your phone number, home address and ID numbers before pasting text into any tool, and check the provider's privacy settings. Add contact details back in your own document afterwards.

faq.q: Can AI invent experience that I then use by mistake?
faq.a: Yes. Assistants sometimes add plausible but false details. Prevent this by instructing it to use only your facts, and then compare every line with your original. Delete anything that you did not provide or cannot defend in an interview.

title: PDF vs DOCX Resume: Which File Format Should You Send?
excerpt: PDF or DOCX for your resume? Compare formatting, ATS compatibility, editing and employer instructions, and learn how to export and check your file correctly.
seo_title: PDF vs DOCX Resume: Which File Format to Send
seo_description: Should you send your resume as PDF or DOCX? Compare layout stability, ATS readability and editing, and learn how to export, name and check your file.
content:
If the employer does not specify a format, send your resume as a PDF exported from a text-based editor. It keeps your layout stable and its text can be read by most systems. If the posting asks for DOCX or if the application form only accepts it, use DOCX. Whatever you choose, make sure the text is selectable and the file name is professional.

## Why the file format matters

Your resume has to survive three journeys: upload into an application system, display on a recruiter's device and sometimes printing. Each format handles those journeys differently. A good choice protects your layout and ensures your text is readable by software and by people.

The right answer also depends on instructions. Employers know their own systems and workflows best, so their request outranks any general rule.

## PDF and DOCX compared

### PDF: strengths and limits

**Strengths**

- **Layout stability:** fonts, spacing and page breaks look the same on any device.
- **Professional look:** it signals a finished document.
- **Harder to alter accidentally:** your formatting is not changed when someone opens it on another machine.
- **Widely accepted:** most application systems take PDFs.

**Limits**

- **Editing:** recruiters or agencies who want to reformat your resume cannot do so easily.
- **Scanned or image PDFs:** if the PDF is only a picture of text, software cannot read it.
- **Odd exports:** some design tools produce PDFs with text broken into pieces or in the wrong order.

A good PDF is created by exporting or saving from a word processor or resume builder, not by taking a screenshot or scanning a printout.

### DOCX: strengths and limits

**Strengths**

- **Editable:** staffing agencies and recruiters can adjust it if needed.
- **Clearly text-based:** parsing is generally straightforward.
- **Requested in some postings:** some systems or recruiters specifically ask for it.

**Limits**

- **Layout shifts:** fonts that are not installed on the recipient's machine are replaced, which can change spacing and page breaks.
- **Version differences:** different word processors may display the same file differently.
- **Accidental edits:** content can be changed by mistake.

If you use DOCX, stick to standard fonts and simple formatting, and review the file in more than one viewer if possible.

## A simple decision guide

| Situation | Suggested format |
|---|---|
| The posting asks for a specific format | Use exactly what they ask |
| No instructions, applying directly or by email | PDF |
| Working with a recruiter or agency | Ask; DOCX is sometimes preferred |
| Application form accepts only certain types | Use an accepted type |
| Resume is a scan or image | Re-create it as a text-based document |

When unsure, you can write to the recruiter: "Would you prefer a PDF or Word version of my resume?" Asking politely is acceptable and shows care.

## How to export a clean PDF

1. Finish and proofread in your editor or the [resume builder](/resume-builder).
2. Use "Save as PDF" or "Export as PDF" rather than printing to an image.
3. Open the exported file and scroll through every page.
4. Try selecting and copying text from the PDF. It should paste in the right order.
5. Check that links are clickable if you included them.
6. Confirm the page count and where the page breaks fall.

A plain-text paste test is a quick way to spot reading-order problems before you upload. The [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can also confirm that your file's text is readable.

## Naming and metadata

Use a simple name:

- Good: `firstname-lastname-resume.pdf`
- Good: `firstname-lastname-resume-marketing.pdf` for a role-specific version
- Avoid: `resume-final-FINAL2.pdf`, `Untitled.pdf`, or someone else's name from an old template

Also check the document properties. Some editors store the previous title or author name inside the file. Clear anything outdated or irrelevant before you send it.

### Other file types to avoid

- **Images (PNG or JPG):** not readable by software and hard for people to use.
- **Pages or other less common formats:** recipients may not be able to open them.
- **Cloud links without file attachments:** these may fail due to permissions or blocked access.
- **Password-protected files:** they block parsing and annoy recruiters.

### A short prompt for file checks

You can ask an assistant to help you organise a final checklist, though the actual file test should be done by you.

```
Create a pre-send checklist for my resume file. Include checks for file
type, file name, selectable text, page count, page breaks, working links,
and document properties. Keep it to 10 items, phrased as yes/no questions.
```

Then run through it with the real file in front of you.

### Mobile and print considerations

Many recruiters review applications on phones or tablets. A PDF with a simple single-column layout scales better than a complex multi-column design. If you print your resume for interviews, print a test page and check that fonts and margins look right. Our article on common resume mistakes covers other final checks.

## What about online application forms that parse your resume?

Many application sites ask you to upload a file and then pre-fill fields such as work history and education from it. After the upload, always review the pre-filled fields carefully. Parsers sometimes split a job title across fields, misread dates or place a skill under the wrong heading. Correct anything that is off before you submit, because those fields may be what a recruiter sees first.

If the system offers to let you type the details manually, consider doing so for important sections. Keep a plain-text version of your resume handy for copying and pasting into text boxes. It saves time and ensures the same wording everywhere.

### Keep versions organised

Create a simple folder system: one master document, then separate PDF exports for each role, named with the company or job type. Record which version you sent to which employer in a short tracking list. When you get a call, you will know exactly what the recruiter has in front of them, and you will avoid mixing up tailored details between applications.

### When the system rejects your file

Occasionally an upload fails or the preview looks wrong. Check the file size, because very large files with embedded images may be refused. Remove unnecessary graphics, re-export and try again. If a field shows scrambled text, your layout may contain columns or text boxes that confuse the parser, so simplify the design and test the plain-text paste again. If nothing works, contact the employer politely and ask whether you may email the file instead. Most recruiters would rather solve a technical issue than lose a good candidate.

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring the employer's instructions.** Follow them exactly.
- **Sending a scanned copy.** Always use a text-based file.
- **Using unusual fonts in DOCX.** Stick to common ones.
- **Skipping the open-and-scroll check.** Layout problems often show only after export.
- **Using sloppy file names.** They make you look disorganised.
- **Attaching multiple versions.** Send only the one requested.
- **Forgetting links.** Test every hyperlink after export.

## Next steps

Build and export a clean file with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), pick a tidy layout from the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and verify readability with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) before you upload.

faq.q: Is PDF or DOCX better for a resume?
faq.a: Follow the employer's instructions first. If none are given, a PDF exported from a text-based editor is usually a safe choice because it preserves layout. Some application systems or recruiters prefer DOCX, so check the posting carefully.

faq.q: Can applicant tracking systems read PDFs?
faq.a: Most modern systems can read text-based PDFs, but scanned or image-only PDFs cannot be parsed reliably. Check that you can select and copy text from your file. If you cannot, the system may not read it either.

faq.q: Should I send a Google Docs link instead of a file?
faq.a: Usually not. Upload a file unless asked for a link. Links can fail because of permissions, and many systems expect an attachment. If you must share a link, test it in a private browsing window first.

faq.q: What should I name my resume file?
faq.a: Use a clear, professional name such as firstname-lastname-resume.pdf. Avoid words like final, new or v3, and avoid spaces and special characters if possible. A tidy name makes your file easy to identify in a recruiter's folder.

title: How to Explain an Employment Gap on Your Resume Honestly
excerpt: Handle a career break on your resume with honest, simple wording. Learn when to mention a gap, how to format dates, what to add and how to talk about it.
seo_title: How to Explain an Employment Gap on Your Resume
seo_description: Explain an employment gap on your resume honestly and briefly. Get wording examples, date formatting tips, ways to show recent learning and interview advice.
content:
To explain an employment gap on your resume, use accurate dates, add one short neutral line describing the period if it is longer than a few months, and show anything relevant you did during that time. Do not hide or alter dates. Most employers care less about the gap itself than about whether you present it clearly and are ready to work now.

## Why gaps are more common than you think

People step away from work for many reasons: study, caring for family, health, relocation, redundancy, travel, a business that did not work out or a slow job market. Recruiters see these situations often. A gap on its own is rarely the problem. The problem is an unexplained or evasive gap, which makes a reader wonder.

Your goal is to give just enough information to remove doubt, keep it factual and steer attention to your current readiness and skills.

## Decide whether the gap needs mentioning

Use these guidelines:

- **Under about three months:** often needs no explanation. Listing years only for each job is acceptable if it is not misleading.
- **Several months to a year:** a simple line is helpful, particularly if it is between recent roles.
- **More than a year:** include a clear line and any relevant activity during that time.

If you list months in dates, a gap will show. If you list only years, the gap may be less visible, but make sure you are not hiding it deceptively. If asked in an interview, you should be able to explain exact dates comfortably.

## Wording options for different situations

Keep it short and neutral. Examples:

- **Career break for caregiving:** "Career break, 2022 to 2024: full-time family caregiving."
- **Study:** "Full-time study, 2023: completed a certificate in [subject]."
- **Redundancy and job search:** "Career transition, 2023: job search and professional development."
- **Health (if you choose to share):** "Career break, 2022 to 2023: personal reasons." You do not have to give medical detail.
- **Relocation:** "Relocated to [city/country], 2023, and completed [course or freelance projects]."
- **Self-employment or freelance:** "Freelance [service], 2022 to 2024" with a couple of real client projects.

You decide how much to share. Privacy is legitimate; a short, non-specific line is fine.

## Where to place the line

In a reverse-chronological resume, add the break as its own entry in the work history, in order with your jobs:

```
Career Break | Jan 2023 – Aug 2024
- Full-time family caregiving
- Completed an online course in [subject] and built [small project]
```

Alternatively, if you prefer not to create an entry, add a short note in your summary or cover letter. The important point is that the timeline remains clear and honest.

### Show recent, relevant activity

If you did anything related to your field, include it. Options:

- Online courses or certifications, with provider and date
- Volunteer work, even a few hours a week
- Freelance or contract tasks, with one or two bullets each
- Personal projects, such as a portfolio, blog, small app or study group
- Industry reading, events or professional memberships (list only if meaningful)

Each should be written like any other entry: an action verb, what you did and what resulted. For example: "Volunteered as a weekend tutor for primary school maths, planning short weekly sessions for a group of children."

### Strengthen the top of the resume

When you have a gap, the summary and skills sections carry extra weight. A concise summary can say you are returning after a break, name your strengths and show your direction:

> Experienced office administrator returning to work after a two-year career break. Skilled in scheduling, record-keeping and customer communication. Recently completed a course in spreadsheet software and am seeking a part-time administration role.

Use a keyword-aware skills section to show up-to-date tools. The guide on finding keywords in a job description can help you identify which tools to emphasise, and the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can highlight any missing terms.

## Use the cover letter for context

A cover letter gives you a few sentences to put your gap in context without letting it dominate. Keep it forward-looking:

> After a two-year break to care for a family member, I am returning to work and have refreshed my skills with a short course in data entry and spreadsheet use. I am excited to bring my organisation and reliability to your team.

The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can help you structure a brief, confident letter.

### A prompt to help you word it

```
I have an employment gap from [dates] because of [reason, in your own words,
share only what you are comfortable with]. During that time I [list any real
activities]. Suggest three short, neutral, honest ways to describe this on a
resume and one version for a cover letter. Do not invent activities,
courses or dates. Keep each version under 25 words.
```

Choose the option that feels truthful and comfortable.

## Prepare your interview answer

Plan a short answer with three parts:

1. **What happened:** one calm sentence.
2. **What you did:** relevant activity or how you stayed prepared.
3. **Why you are ready:** your motivation for this role now.

Example: "I took 18 months out to look after a family member. During that time I completed a bookkeeping course, and I am now ready to return full-time and keen to use those skills."

Practise saying it aloud. Avoid long apologies or excessive detail, and do not criticise past employers.

### Formatting choices that help

- Keep to a standard reverse-chronological layout so recruiters can see your timeline.
- Use consistent date formatting.
- Avoid functional layouts that hide dates, since they may increase suspicion. Our article on resume formats explains the trade-offs.
- Keep the document to one or two pages and put your strongest, most recent evidence at the top.

### Staying current during a search

If you are still between jobs, treat the time as active preparation. Set a small weekly routine: one hour of learning a tool listed in your target postings, one hour on a practice project and a few applications tailored to specific roles. Keep short notes on what you finish. These notes become honest, concrete lines for your resume and give you real answers when an interviewer asks what you have been doing.

Networking helps as well. Contact former colleagues, join a professional group or attend free events in your field. Many people find roles through someone who already knows their work, and a gap matters far less once a person can vouch for you.

## Common mistakes

- **Altering dates.** It is dishonest and risky.
- **Over-explaining.** One line is usually enough.
- **Apologising.** Avoid phrases like "unfortunately" or "I was unable to".
- **Leaving a blank.** A silent gap invites assumptions.
- **Listing irrelevant filler.** Include activities that show skills or responsibility.
- **Skipping a refresh of skills.** Even a short course or project shows commitment.
- **Not practising the interview answer.** Prepare so you sound calm and confident.

## Next steps

Update your timeline in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), pick a straightforward layout from the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and write a short, positive letter in the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

faq.q: Do I have to explain every gap on my resume?
faq.a: Short gaps of a few months can usually be covered by listing years instead of months. Longer gaps are better acknowledged with one neutral line so the reader is not left guessing. You are not obliged to share private details.

faq.q: Should I hide a gap by changing dates?
faq.a: No. Altering dates is dishonest, and it is easy to uncover during reference or background checks. Use honest dates and present the gap clearly and briefly, then focus attention on what you did and what you can offer now.

faq.q: What can I put in a gap period?
faq.a: Anything that is real and relevant: study, courses, caring responsibilities, volunteering, freelance projects, travel with a learning component or personal projects. Describe it plainly in one line and add bullets only if it supports the job.

faq.q: How do I answer gap questions in an interview?
faq.a: Be brief, calm and truthful. State the reason in a sentence, say what you did to stay current, and move to why you are ready now. Practise aloud so you do not over-explain or sound apologetic.

title: Resume Projects Section: How to Write Entries That Impress
excerpt: Add a resume projects section that proves your skills. Learn what to include, how to format entries and see honest bullet examples for students.
seo_title: Resume Projects Section: How to Write Strong Entries
seo_description: Write a resume projects section that shows real skills. Learn what to include, how to format each entry and see honest examples for students and switchers.
content:
A resume projects section should list two to four relevant projects, each with a title, context, dates, the tools or methods you used and two or three bullets about what you personally did and produced. Add a link when the work is public. It is one of the best ways to prove skills when your job history is short or in a different field.

## When a projects section helps most

Projects matter most when you need to prove ability without a long work history:

- **Students and freshers** who have coursework and personal builds rather than jobs
- **Career changers** who have started practising skills in the new field
- **Self-taught people** whose learning happened outside formal roles
- **Specialists** such as developers, designers, writers and analysts, where samples are expected

For experienced professionals, a projects section can still help if it shows a skill that your jobs did not, but it should sit below your work history.

## What counts as a project

A project is any piece of work with a goal, a process and an outcome. It does not have to be impressive in scale. Valid examples include:

- A class assignment with a real deliverable, such as a report, model, app or presentation
- A personal site, app, blog or newsletter
- A data analysis of a public dataset
- A volunteer or community task, such as designing a poster set or organising a fundraiser
- A freelance job for a small business or relative
- A competition or hackathon entry
- A study group, tutoring programme or workshop you created

If you can say what the goal was, what you did and what resulted, it can be a project.

## The format of a project entry

Use a consistent structure:

```
Project Title | Context (course, personal, volunteer) | Month Year
Tools: [list of key tools or methods]
- Action verb + what you did + how + result or output
- Action verb + what you did + how + result or output
- Link or location of the work, if public
```

Keep each bullet to one or two lines. Put the most relevant project first.

## Example entries

### A data analysis project

```
Public Transport Usage Analysis | Statistics course | Nov 2025
Tools: Spreadsheet software, charts
- Cleaned and organised a public dataset of weekly ridership figures, removing duplicate and incomplete rows
- Built three charts comparing usage by day and season, and wrote a two-page summary of the patterns found
- Presented findings to a class of 30 and answered questions about the method
```

### A writing project

```
Beginner's Guide to Budgeting | Personal blog | 2025
- Researched and wrote a 1,500-word guide with examples and a printable template
- Edited the piece after feedback from two readers and improved the structure and headings
```

### A community project

```
Neighbourhood Book Swap | Volunteer | Spring 2025
- Organised a monthly book swap, recruiting four volunteers and promoting it with printed posters and social posts
- Kept a simple log of donations and attendance in a spreadsheet to plan the next events
```

Notice each example describes real actions, tools and outputs. Only include figures that you can verify. Replace sample details with your own.

## Be clear about your role

For group projects, state your part precisely. "Built the login page and tested it with five users" is more credible than "Worked on a web app". If you led the group, say what you coordinated. If you contributed a single component, name it. Interviewers often ask follow-up questions, and clarity protects you.

## Choose projects that match the job

Review the job description. Which skills does it stress? Pick projects that show those skills and put them first. A project that demonstrates analysis, communication and meeting a deadline is relevant to many roles, even if the topic differs.

You can also reword the project entry to use the employer's terms where they truthfully describe your work. Our guide on finding keywords in a job description walks through the method, and the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can show which terms from a posting are missing from your text.

### Where to place the section

- **Early in your career:** place Projects right after Education, or even before it.
- **Career changers:** place it after your summary and key skills, before older unrelated roles if the projects are strongly relevant.
- **Experienced professionals:** place it after Work Experience.

Keep it to what fits on your page length. A one-page resume leaves room for two or three entries.

### Showing links responsibly

If you include links, check that:

- They open without needing a login.
- The page or repository is tidy, with a short description of the project.
- The work shown matches what you claim on the resume.
- You are comfortable with a recruiter viewing everything linked.

Write the link as plain readable text, for example a short portfolio address, in addition to any clickable text, so it remains useful when printed.

### A prompt to polish your project entries

```
Below are notes about my projects. For each, write a resume entry with a title
line and 2-3 bullets starting with strong action verbs. Use only the facts I
give. Do not add tools, numbers, outcomes or links I did not mention. Where
a detail would improve the entry (scope, tools used, result), list a
question for me to answer instead of guessing.

Target role: [job title]
Project notes: [paste]
```

Always check each bullet against reality before you use it.

### Presenting unfinished or private work

Not all projects are finished or public. You can still list an in-progress project if you label it honestly, for example "In progress" with the current stage. For private or confidential work, describe the type of task and your role without sharing sensitive data. Offer to discuss details in an interview.

### Turning a vague project into a strong entry

Start with a rough note such as "made a website for a club". Ask yourself a few questions: who was it for, what problem did it solve, what did you build and with which tools, what did you personally do, and how did people use it? The answers might become: "Built a three-page website for a university photography club using a website builder, wrote the content and added an event signup form that the committee used each semester."

Every extra detail is a fact about your work, not decoration. If you cannot answer a question honestly, leave that detail out. A short, accurate entry is better than a long one that stretches the truth.

## Common mistakes

- **Listing project names without descriptions.** A title alone says nothing.
- **Including too many small items.** Select the strongest few.
- **Not describing your own role.** Make your contribution clear.
- **Exaggerating scale.** Use real details and avoid inflated claims.
- **Adding broken or messy links.** Test them and tidy the destination.
- **Using jargon without context.** Explain tools and outcomes in plain terms.
- **Forgetting to update.** Replace older, weaker entries with recent, stronger ones.

## Next steps

Add your best projects in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), choose a one-page layout from the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and test your final file with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker).

faq.q: Should I include personal projects on my resume?
faq.a: Yes, if they show skills relevant to the job. Personal projects are especially valuable for students, freshers and career changers. Include the ones that match the role, describe what you did and add a link if the work is publicly viewable.

faq.q: How many projects should I list?
faq.a: Two to four is usually enough. Choose the most relevant and substantial, and give each two or three bullets. A long list of small items looks scattered and takes space from stronger evidence.

faq.q: Can I include class projects?
faq.a: Yes. Academic projects count as real evidence when you explain the goal, your role, the tools and the output. State clearly what you personally did, especially in group work, and avoid inflating the scale.

faq.q: Do I need a link for each project?
faq.a: Links help when the work is public and tidy, such as a repository, portfolio page or published article. If the work is private or unfinished, describe it clearly instead. Make sure any link you add works and represents you well.

title: Cover Letter Opening Lines: Examples for Different Situations
excerpt: Start your cover letter well with opening lines for common situations: referrals, career changes, entry-level roles and more, plus patterns to avoid.
seo_title: Cover Letter Opening Lines: Examples That Work
seo_description: Write a strong first paragraph for your cover letter. See opening line examples for referrals, career changes and entry-level roles, plus patterns to avoid.
content:
A good cover letter opening names the role, states one specific reason you fit it and sets up the rest of the letter in two to four sentences. Skip generic lines like "I am writing to express my interest" in favour of a concrete credential, project or connection. Below are patterns and examples for common situations, which you can adapt with your own true details.

## What an opening needs to do

A hiring manager may read dozens of letters. The first lines decide whether they read the rest with interest. A good opening does three things:

1. **Identifies the role**, so there is no doubt what you are applying for.
2. **Gives a reason to keep reading**, usually a relevant skill, result or connection.
3. **Sounds like a real person**, in a professional tone.

It does not need a gimmick. Specificity is the most reliable hook.

## The basic pattern

> I would like to apply for the [role] position at [company]. [One sentence about your most relevant experience, skill or project], which matches [specific requirement or interest from the posting].

Everything below is a variation on this pattern.

## Examples by situation

### You have directly relevant experience

> I would like to apply for the Customer Support Specialist role at [Company]. In my current position handling billing and delivery queries by chat and phone, I have learned how to resolve issues clearly and calmly, which is the focus of your posting.

### You were referred by someone

Only mention a referral if the person agreed and the connection is real.

> [Name], a [role] on your [team], suggested I apply for the Marketing Coordinator position. After speaking with them about the team's approach to beginner-friendly content, I was keen to contribute my experience planning and scheduling content for a student society.

### You are a student or fresher

> I am a final-year business student applying for the Operations Intern position. Through a university project analysing delivery times for a local business and a part-time role in retail, I have built practical skills in spreadsheets, reporting and customer communication that match your requirements.

### You are changing careers

> I would like to apply for the Learning and Development Coordinator role. Over five years as a primary school teacher, I designed and delivered lessons for mixed-ability groups and tracked progress carefully. I have since completed a short course in instructional design and built a sample training module, and I am eager to apply these skills in a corporate setting.

### You are returning after a break

> I am excited to apply for the Administrative Assistant role at [Company]. After a two-year career break, I have refreshed my skills with a course in spreadsheet software and am ready to bring my organisation and reliability back to a team.

### You are responding to a company's work or mission

Be accurate and specific about what you noticed.

> I would like to apply for the Content Writer position. I was interested to see that your blog publishes step-by-step guides for new users, as I enjoy turning complex topics into clear instructions, something I practised in a study guide series I wrote for my course.

### You have a relevant project rather than a job

> I would like to apply for the Junior Data Analyst role. For my final-year project, I cleaned a public dataset, built a set of charts and presented the findings to a panel, which gave me practical experience in the analysis and reporting tasks described in your posting.

Replace all details with your own real ones. If something in an example is not true for you, change it.

## Patterns to avoid

- **"To Whom It May Concern"** when a name is easy to find.
- **"I am writing to express my interest..." with nothing after it.** It adds no information.
- **"I am a hard-working, passionate team player."** Anyone can write that.
- **Beginning with an apology or lack of experience.** Lead with what you can offer.
- **Overly dramatic hooks.** Claims like "I will be the best hire you ever make" read as empty.
- **Quoting a famous person.** Unless it directly relates to the job, skip it.
- **Starting with the company's history.** The employer knows it; tell them what you bring.

## How to find a specific hook

Use a three-step method:

1. Look at the top two or three requirements in the posting.
2. Find your closest real example for each.
3. Choose the strongest and put it in your first or second sentence.

If you are unsure, ask yourself: what would make a busy hiring manager want to read paragraph two?

### A prompt to generate options

```
Write five different opening paragraphs (2-3 sentences each) for a cover letter
for the role of [job title] at [company]. Use only the facts below. Each
opening should use a different angle: (1) relevant experience, (2) a project,
(3) interest in the company's work, (4) a skill matched to the posting,
(5) a concise direct statement. Avoid clichés like "passionate" and "perfect
fit", and do not invent facts.

Job requirements: [paste main points]
My facts: [paste real experience and projects]
What I know about the company: [paste accurate details]
```

Pick the one that sounds most like you and adjust the wording. You can then assemble the full letter in the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

## Make the opening match your resume

The opening should align with your resume's summary and top bullets. If your resume emphasises data analysis, do not open the letter with customer service unless that is truly your focus. Consistency makes your application feel coherent. You can check your resume's alignment with the posting using the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker).

### Tone and length

Keep the tone warm and professional. A confident, plain style beats flowery language. Avoid more than four sentences before you get to your evidence. For the whole letter's structure, see our guide to cover letter structure.

## Common mistakes

- **Making the opening about yourself only.** Link it to the employer's needs.
- **Being vague.** Name the role and a concrete example.
- **Copying sample lines verbatim.** Adapt them to your facts and voice.
- **Claiming a referral without permission.** Always confirm first.
- **Stuffing in too many claims.** Choose one strong point.
- **Forgetting to update the company and role.** A wrong name in the first line can end your application.
- **Using a tone that does not fit the field.** Match the culture without losing professionalism.

## Next steps

Draft your opening in the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder), make sure your [resume](/resume-builder) supports the same story and browse more writing prompts in the [careers prompt library](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: How should I start a cover letter?
faq.a: Begin with the role you are applying for and one specific reason you fit it, such as a relevant project, skill or experience. Keep it to two or three sentences. Avoid generic lines that could open any letter.

faq.q: Is it okay to start with 'I am writing to apply'?
faq.a: It is acceptable but forgettable. Because it carries no information beyond the obvious, you can replace it with a sentence that names the role and your strongest relevant credential. Clarity matters more than a clever hook.

faq.q: Should my opening be creative or funny?
faq.a: Only if it suits the field and you can do it well. Most roles reward a clear, confident, specific opening. A short personal or story-led opening can work in creative fields, but it still needs to connect to the job.

faq.q: How long should the first paragraph be?
faq.a: Two to four sentences is plenty. The opening should name the role, state your fit and set up the rest of the letter. Save the detailed stories for the following paragraphs so the reader reaches the evidence quickly.

title: Resume Education and Certifications Section: Format and Examples
excerpt: List degrees, courses and certifications on your resume correctly. Learn what to include, how to order entries, how to handle unfinished degrees and more.
seo_title: Resume Education and Certifications: Format and Examples
seo_description: Format your resume education and certifications clearly. Learn what to include, how to order entries and how to list unfinished degrees and online courses.
content:
On your resume, list education with the degree, institution and graduation date, and list certifications with the name, issuer and year, placing whichever section is strongest for the job first. Keep entries brief and consistent, include only relevant courses, and describe unfinished studies honestly. This section should confirm your qualifications quickly, not take up valuable space.

## What this section is for

Recruiters use the education and certification sections to confirm basic requirements: the degree a job asks for, a licence or a recognised credential. For early-career applicants, these sections also provide evidence of knowledge. For experienced professionals, they usually play a supporting role.

The best approach is to be accurate, easy to scan and relevant to the job.

## Where to place it

- **Students and recent graduates:** place Education near the top, below the summary.
- **Experienced professionals:** place it after Work Experience.
- **Career changers with new qualifications:** place education or certifications higher if they are the key link to the new field.
- **Roles requiring a licence or certification:** make that credential easy to see, near the top or in a clear dedicated section.
