If you are unsure, ask which entry would most quickly answer the recruiter's first question about your qualifications.

## How to format an education entry

Use a consistent pattern:

```
Degree or qualification, Major | Institution, City, Country
Graduation date (or expected date)
Optional: relevant coursework, honours, thesis or key project
```

Example:

```
BSc Business Administration | University of [Name], [City]
Graduated June 2025
Relevant coursework: Marketing Principles, Business Statistics, Operations Management
Final-year project: Customer survey analysis for a local retailer
```

Keep optional lines to what helps the target role. Experienced professionals can often reduce education to a single line.

### What to add and what to leave out

**Often worth adding**
- Relevant coursework (four to six items)
- Honours, distinctions or scholarships you actually earned
- A thesis or major project connected to the job
- GPA or marks, if requested or strong

**Often worth leaving out**
- Every module you have taken
- GPA or marks that are unremarkable, unless asked
- High school information, once you have post-secondary education
- Irrelevant awards from many years ago

## Handling unfinished or ongoing studies

Honesty is essential. Use these approaches:

- **Currently studying:** "BSc Computer Science, [University] | Expected June 2027."
- **Studied but did not complete:** "Studied [subject] at [Institution], 2021 to 2023" with relevant courses or credits if applicable. Do not write the degree name in a way that suggests completion.
- **Transferred or paused:** list what is true and brief, and explain in an interview if asked.
- **Self-taught:** use a "Training and courses" section for relevant programs, and focus on projects and skills.

Employers often verify education, so accuracy protects you.

## Certifications and courses

For certifications, include:

- **Name of the certification**
- **Issuing organisation**
- **Date earned** (and expiry date if relevant)
- **Credential or licence number** only if the employer asks

Example:

```
CERTIFICATIONS
Project Management Foundations | [Provider] | 2025
First Aid Certificate | [Organisation] | 2024, valid until 2027
Google Sheets for Data Analysis (online course) | [Provider] | 2025
```

Check the provider's official site for the correct name of the credential. Keep the list focused on items that match the job. Ten loosely related certificates are less persuasive than three relevant ones.

### Online courses

Online learning can be valuable, especially for career changers. To make it count:

- List course name, provider and year.
- Add one line on what you built or applied, if anything.
- Group several related short courses into one line, such as "Short courses: SQL basics, data visualisation, spreadsheet functions".
- Avoid claiming expertise from a short introductory course. Use words like "foundations" or "introductory" if that is accurate.

## Order of entries

Within each section, use reverse-chronological order, with the most recent first, unless a particular credential is far more relevant than a newer one. Keep dates in the same format as elsewhere on the resume.

### Make the section ATS-friendly

- Use standard headings: "Education" and "Certifications" (or "Licences and Certifications").
- Write the degree in full or in both forms where helpful, such as "Bachelor of Science (BSc)".
- Put dates on the same line or next line in a consistent pattern.
- Avoid placing education in a sidebar, text box or graphic.

You can check how your sections read to software with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker), and see ready-made layouts in the [resume templates](/resume-templates).

### A prompt to format your entries

```
Format my education and certifications for a resume. Use a consistent
pattern, reverse-chronological order and plain text. Use only the details
I provide. If something is unfinished, label it honestly. Tell me which
items seem least relevant to the role of [job title] so I can decide
whether to cut them.

My details: [paste]
```

Review the output for accuracy before you copy it into your resume.

### Special cases

- **International qualifications:** add a short equivalent note only if the employer needs it, and be accurate.
- **Professional licences:** put them in a dedicated section if the role requires them.
- **Continuing education:** group recent training under "Professional development".
- **Expired certifications:** include only if relevant and mark them honestly, or leave them out.

### Two worked examples

#### A recent graduate

```
EDUCATION
BA Economics | University of [Name], [City] | Graduated 2025
Relevant coursework: Microeconomics, Econometrics, Data Analysis
Dissertation: Household spending patterns in [region] (public data)

CERTIFICATIONS
Spreadsheet Analysis (online course) | [Provider] | 2025
```

The graduate leads with the degree, adds a few relevant courses and a dissertation line, and includes one targeted course that supports the data skills the job asks for.

#### An experienced professional

```
EDUCATION
MBA | [Institution] | 2018
BSc Engineering | [Institution] | 2012

CERTIFICATIONS
Project Management Professional | [Issuer] | 2020
```

Here education is compact because work experience carries the story. Only credentials that matter for the target role remain.

### Keeping credentials current and verifiable

Employers may confirm your qualifications, so keep your certificates, transcripts and credential links in one folder. Note renewal dates for any licence or certification that expires, and update your resume as soon as you renew or complete something new. If a credential has a public verification page, you can mention that it can be verified, but only if the issuer provides one.

## Common mistakes

- **Listing too much.** Select what supports the role.
- **Being vague about unfinished degrees.** State the status clearly.
- **Inconsistent formats.** Keep dates and punctuation uniform.
- **Including irrelevant certificates.** Prioritise by relevance.
- **Using unclear abbreviations.** Spell out less common terms.
- **Forgetting to update.** Add new credentials and remove outdated ones.
- **Embellishing.** Never inflate titles, honours or completion status.

## Next steps

Enter your details in the [resume builder](/resume-builder), choose a clear layout from the [resume templates](/resume-templates) and confirm everything reads correctly using the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker).

faq.q: Should education go before or after experience?
faq.a: If you have relevant work experience, put it first and keep education short. If you are a student, recent graduate or career changer whose degree is your strongest credential, lead with education. Choose the order that shows your best evidence first.

faq.q: How do I list a degree I have not finished?
faq.a: List the institution, program and the years attended, and add "expected" with a graduation date if you are still studying. If you did not finish, you can write "coursework completed" or relevant credits. Do not imply that you earned a degree you did not.

faq.q: Do online course certificates belong on a resume?
faq.a: Yes, if they are relevant to the job and from a recognised provider. List the course name, provider and year. For many courses, one line is enough. Prioritise those that match the posting, and leave out unrelated or outdated ones.

faq.q: Should I include my high school?
faq.a: Usually not once you have started a degree or have work experience. If high school is your highest qualification, list it. For early students, a short entry can be fine until you have more recent items to replace it.

title: Resume Header and Contact Details: What to Include and Skip
excerpt: Set up the top of your resume correctly: name, email, phone, location, links and what to leave out. Includes examples, privacy tips and ATS-friendly formatting.
seo_title: Resume Header and Contact Details: What to Include
seo_description: Get the top of your resume right. Learn which contact details to include, how to format links and location, what to skip for privacy and ATS-safe header tips.
content:
The top of your resume should show your full name, a professional email address, a phone number, your city and region and, if useful, one or two links to a portfolio or professional profile. Skip your full street address, date of birth and other private details unless the employer requires them. Put this information in the main body, not in the page header, so it can be read reliably.

## Why the header deserves attention

It sounds simple, but the header is the one place where an error can block everything else. A mistyped email or phone number means a recruiter cannot reach you, no matter how strong your resume is. A messy header also creates a poor first impression, and a header built in a way that software cannot read can lead to a blank contact record in an application system.

A good header is short, accurate and easy to find.

## The essentials

### Full name

Use the name you will use professionally and that matches your application forms and profiles. Make it the largest text on the page, but within reason. If you commonly go by a shortened or different name, you can use that, as long as it is consistent across your documents and online profiles.

### Email address

Use a professional address, ideally based on your name, such as a simple firstname-lastname pattern. Avoid nicknames, jokes or old school addresses. Check that you can access it regularly and that the spam filter does not capture replies.

### Phone number

Include one number you answer or can return calls on promptly. If you are applying internationally, include the country code. Make sure your voicemail greeting is professional and the mailbox is not full.

### Location

City and region or country are usually enough. They help employers judge location and time zone without exposing your full address. If you are open to relocating or applying for remote roles, you can add a short note such as "Open to relocation" or "Available for remote work" only if it is true.

### Links

Add links only if they strengthen your application:

- A professional profile with up-to-date experience
- A portfolio, personal website or project repository
- A published writing portfolio

Make sure each link works, opens without a login and shows work you are proud of. Use short, tidy addresses. If a link would show something unprofessional or empty, leave it out.

## Example headers

**Simple and ATS-friendly**

```
Firstname Lastname
City, Country | name@email.com | +00 000 000 0000
portfolio-address | professional-profile-address
```

**With a role headline**

```
Firstname Lastname
Junior Data Analyst
City, Country | name@email.com | +00 000 000 0000
```

A short headline below your name can clarify your target, but it should match the job and your summary.

## What to leave out

- **Full street address:** not needed for most applications and a privacy risk.
- **Date of birth, age, marital status and similar personal details:** unnecessary in many countries and can lead to bias. Include them only if the employer or local convention requires.
- **Photo:** customs differ. If you are unsure, leave it out, or follow the employer's instructions.
- **National ID, passport or financial numbers:** never include them on a resume.
- **Social media accounts unrelated to your work:** keep your personal profiles out unless relevant.
- **The word "Resume" or "CV" as a title:** the format makes it obvious and wastes space.
- **Multiple phone numbers or emails:** one of each is enough.

For privacy, think carefully about what you place in a document that may be stored in many systems or shared widely.

## Make the header readable by software

- Put the name and contact line in the **main body** of the page rather than in the page header or footer area, where some systems do not look.
- Avoid icons in place of words. A small phone icon is fine if the number is also written in text, but avoid using only icons or images.
- Use plain text separators, such as a vertical bar or comma, between items.
- Avoid placing contact details in a table, text box or sidebar.
- Keep fonts and sizes simple.

The [resume templates](/resume-templates) are structured so the contact information sits in the main flow of the document, and the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can show whether your text is read in a sensible order.

## Keep your online presence consistent

Recruiters may look you up. Make sure your professional profile matches your resume: the same job titles, dates and main claims. Update your headline and summary to reflect the roles you want, and set your public details to what you are comfortable sharing. A resume and a profile that contradict each other raise questions.

### A prompt to review your header

```
Review the header of my resume below. Check for: unprofessional wording,
missing essentials, details I should remove for privacy, inconsistent
formatting, and anything that might not be read correctly by software.
Suggest fixes, but do not invent any contact details or links.

[PASTE YOUR HEADER TEXT, WITH CONTACT DETAILS REPLACED BY PLACEHOLDERS]
```

For privacy, replace real phone numbers and addresses with placeholders when sharing text with any tool.

### Additional tips

- **Test your email.** Send yourself a message and check it arrives and looks fine.
- **Check your links in a private window.** Make sure no login is needed.
- **Be consistent across documents.** Use the same header on your resume and cover letter. The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) keeps these details aligned.
- **Update when things change.** A new phone number or email should be changed everywhere.
- **Use the right country format.** Write phone numbers in the format recruiters in the target country expect.

### International and remote applications

When you apply across borders, small header choices help recruiters. Write phone numbers with the country code, spell out the country name rather than only a postal abbreviation, and mention your working time zone or work authorisation only if the posting asks or it genuinely matters. Do not claim an authorisation you do not have. If you are relocating, say so in a short, accurate line, such as "Relocating to [city] in [month]", so the employer understands your availability.

For remote roles, a clear location and a note about time-zone overlap can answer a question before it is asked, which keeps your application moving.

## Common mistakes

- **Typos in the email or phone number.** Proofread character by character.
- **Using an unprofessional email address.** Create a new one if necessary.
- **Putting contact details in the page header.** Software may miss them.
- **Adding private details unnecessarily.** Protect your privacy.
- **Linking to empty or messy profiles.** Update before you share.
- **Making the header too large.** It should not take a quarter of the page.
- **Leaving out a location entirely.** Employers often want to know where you are based.

faq.q: What contact details should a resume include?
faq.a: Include your full name, a professional email address, a phone number and your city and country or region. Add a link to a relevant professional profile or portfolio if it strengthens your application. Full street address is not usually needed.

faq.q: Should I put my full home address on my resume?
faq.a: Generally no. City and region are enough for most applications and protect your privacy. Some employers or countries have specific requirements, so follow the application instructions when they ask for more detail.

faq.q: Should I include a photo on my resume?
faq.a: It depends on the country and industry. In some places photos are customary, while in others they are discouraged and can raise bias concerns. If unsure, leave it out, or follow the norms and instructions for the employer and region.

faq.q: Is it a problem to put contact details in the header section?
faq.a: It can be. Some systems skip content in the document header or footer. Put your name and contact line in the main body at the top of the page so that software and people can always find it.
